executive_summary.headline: Anthropic releases Claude Opus 4.8 on May 28 — system card shows lowest misaligned-behavior rate of any production Opus, with parallel subagent dynamic workflows now available in research preview for enterprise and team plans
executive_summary.body: Anthropic published Claude Opus 4.8 on May 28, 2026, alongside the Claude Opus 4.8 System Card. The system card documents that Opus 4.8 reaches new highs on Anthropic's prosocial-traits evaluations and has substantially lower rates of misaligned behavior — deception, cooperation with misuse — than Opus 4.7, comparable to the unreleased Mythos Preview. On the Super-Agent benchmark, Opus 4.8 is the only model to complete every case end-to-end; it scores 84% on Online-Mind2Web and holds the top recorded score on the Legal Agent Benchmark. New enterprise features: Dynamic Workflows (research preview) allows Claude Code to plan and spawn hundreds of parallel subagents in a single session on Enterprise, Team, and Max plans. API pricing is $5/$25 per million input/output tokens; Fast Mode runs at 2.5× speed and is 3× cheaper than previous fast-mode pricing.

executive_summary.headline: EU Digital Omnibus on AI reaches provisional political agreement — high-risk Annex III obligations deferred to December 2, 2027, but Article 50 transparency rules remain enforceable August 2, 2026
executive_summary.body: The EU Council and Parliament reached a provisional political agreement on the Digital Omnibus on AI on May 7, 2026, confirmed by Member State representatives on May 13. Under the agreement, high-risk obligations for stand-alone Annex III AI systems (covering recruitment, credit scoring, education, biometrics, and law enforcement) move from August 2, 2026 to December 2, 2027. AI embedded in Annex I regulated products (medical devices, machinery) moves to August 2, 2028. Formal adoption and Official Journal publication are expected before August 2, 2026; the amended dates do not bind until that publication. Critically, Article 50 transparency obligations — requiring disclosure when interacting with AI systems and machine-readable marking of synthetic content — remain applicable from August 2, 2026 regardless of the Omnibus. A new Article 5 prohibition on AI-generated non-consensual intimate imagery applies from December 2, 2026.

executive_summary.headline: EU Commission opens Article 50 transparency guideline consultation closing June 3 — providers of interactive AI systems and generative AI must implement disclosures and machine-readable marks by August 2, 2026
executive_summary.body: On May 8, 2026, the European Commission published draft guidelines on Article 50 of the EU AI Act, opening a public stakeholder consultation that closes June 3, 2026. The guidelines cover four distinct obligations: providers must disclose AI nature at first interaction with users of interactive systems (chatbots, voice agents, agentic systems) and must embed machine-readable marks in generative AI outputs; deployers must disclose emotion recognition and biometric categorization, and must label deepfakes and AI-generated public-interest text. The guidelines clarify that the same AI system can trigger multiple simultaneous obligations, and that the regime applies extraterritorially when outputs are used in the EU. Penalties for non-compliance reach €15M or 3% of worldwide annual turnover. The consultation closes June 3; the obligations apply August 2.

executive_summary.headline: UK AI Security Institute signs MoU with Australian counterpart on May 25, releasing research showing frontier AI systems are accelerating complex cyber-attack capability
executive_summary.body: UK AI Minister Kanishka Narayan signed a Memorandum of Understanding with Australia's Assistant Minister Dr. Andrew Charlton in Canberra on May 25, 2026, establishing a formal partnership between the UK AI Security Institute (AISI) and the Australian AI Safety Institute. The MoU covers shared research into frontier AI capabilities — including cyber-attack potential — collaborative development of international evaluation best practices, and staff exchanges. Accompanying new AISI research found that advanced AI systems are rapidly improving their ability to carry out complex cyber-attacks, with the institute having previously found that AI models from Anthropic and OpenAI could complete a complex 32-step corporate network attack in a fraction of the time it would take a skilled human.

executive_summary.headline: White House frontier-model executive order remains unsigned after last-minute withdrawal on May 22 — internal conflict between deregulatory and security-review factions cited; no revised timeline announced
executive_summary.body: The Trump administration circulated a draft executive order on AI safety and cybersecurity expected to be signed May 22, 2026, then withdrew it hours before the signing ceremony. The draft would have created a voluntary framework requiring AI developers to submit frontier models to federal review (NSA, CISA, NIST) up to 90 days before public release, plus a separate cybersecurity section directing DoD network hardening and a Treasury AI vulnerability clearinghouse. Reporting from Politico identified an internal split between the White House AI and technology advisor (favoring a deregulatory approach to compete with China) and officials who supported the voluntary review framework. The administration has not announced a revised timeline.

On safety: the card's alignment findings (misaligned-behavior rates comparable to Mythos Preview, lowest incorrect-hallucination rate across tested models) provide the primary-source documentation required for an AI governance review board evaluating whether to expand Anthropic model use. On capability: Dynamic Workflows is the most enterprise-relevant new feature. The pattern — plan a large task, decompose it into hundreds of parallel subagents, verify before surfacing results — maps directly onto document-processing workflows (large contract portfolios, engineering specification reviews, financial model audits) that are too large for a single context window. The regulated-environment caveat: Dynamic Workflows is in research preview, meaning it has not yet gone through full enterprise change-control testing. Run it only in a sandboxed, non-production environment against non-sensitive data until it reaches GA. Data residency commitments under Anthropic's enterprise agreement must be verified before any PII or non-public financial data enters a multi-agent workflow, because subagent spawning may increase the surface area of data exposure. The 30-day experiment: identify one large-document workflow currently done by a team of analysts (e.g., reviewing a set of supplier contracts for AI-related clauses), scope it to 5–10 documents, run it with Dynamic Workflows under a Max plan in an isolated environment, and compare output quality and cycle time against the current human baseline.

top_picks.subtitle: Provisional political agreement May 7, confirmed May 13; formal Official Journal publication expected before August 2, 2026.

top_picks.summary: The EU Council and Parliament reached a provisional political agreement on the Digital Omnibus on AI on May 7, 2026, confirmed by Member State representatives on May 13. Stand-alone high-risk Annex III obligations — covering AI in recruitment, credit scoring, education, biometrics, law enforcement, and border control — are deferred from August 2, 2026 to December 2, 2027. AI embedded in Annex I regulated products (medical devices, machinery, vehicles) moves from August 2027 to August 2028. Article 50 transparency obligations are not deferred: interactive AI system disclosure requirements and synthetic-content marking mandates apply from August 2, 2026. A new Article 5 prohibition on AI-generated non-consensual intimate imagery takes effect December 2, 2026. Formal adoption and Official Journal publication are expected before August 2, 2026; the deferred dates do not bind until publication.
top_picks.recurrence_note: Last week covered the May 19 draft high-risk classification guidelines (different document). This week captures the Omnibus deferral agreement and the August 2 Article 50 live-compliance date.
top_picks.enterprise_adaptation: The Omnibus deferral gives enterprises with EU market exposure more runway for Annex III compliance work — but it does not remove the near-term obligation that now matters most: Article 50 transparency requirements apply August 2, 2026 regardless of the Omnibus. The implementation pattern for an enterprise AI team: (1) triage current EU-facing AI deployments into three buckets — interactive systems (chatbots, voice agents), generative AI producing synthetic content, and systems performing emotion recognition or biometric categorization — because each bucket has distinct obligations under Article 50; (2) for interactive systems, confirm with your AI vendor that the system discloses its non-human nature at first interaction per user, in a manner that is 'clear and distinguishable' per the draft guidelines (not buried in terms); (3) for synthetic-content systems, audit whether your vendor is implementing machine-readable marks (watermarks, metadata, cryptographic provenance) — the guidelines state no single current technique meets all four standards simultaneously, so a combination is required; (4) use the Omnibus deferral for Annex III to conduct your high-risk classification audit methodically rather than under emergency timeline pressure. Regulated-environment caveat: the Omnibus only takes legal effect upon Official Journal publication, which has not occurred as of May 31. Do not treat the deferred dates as final until the text is published. The 30-day experiment: run an Article 50 readiness checklist for your top five EU-facing AI systems before August 2 — map each to its Article 50 obligation category, document vendor confirmations of disclosure implementation, and note any gaps.

top_picks.title: EU Commission Article 50 Transparency Guidelines: Consultation Closes June 3, 2026 — Providers and Deployers of EU-Facing AI Systems Must Be Ready by August 2
top_picks.subtitle: Draft published May 8; covers interactive AI disclosure, synthetic-content marking, deepfake labeling, emotion-recognition notice; penalties up to €15M or 3% of global turnover.
top_picks.author: European Commission AI Office

secondary_urls.label: EC consultation portal — submit feedback until June 3
Pearl Cohen — full breakdown of provider and deployer obligations
Dilr.ai — voice AI deployer checklist with specific Article 50 obligations table

top_picks.summary: The European Commission published 40-page draft guidelines on Article 50 of the EU AI Act on May 8, 2026. The guidelines cover four transparency obligation categories: (1) providers of interactive AI systems must disclose AI nature at first interaction per user; (2) providers of generative AI must embed machine-readable marks (watermarks, metadata, cryptographic provenance, fingerprints) in synthetic outputs — the guidelines acknowledge no single current technique meets all four standards (effectiveness, robustness, reliability, interoperability) simultaneously; (3) deployers must notify users exposed to emotion recognition or biometric categorization; (4) deployers must clearly label deepfakes and AI-generated text on matters of public interest. The regime applies extraterritorially to third-country providers when outputs are used in the EU. The consultation closes June 3; obligations apply August 2, 2026. Penalties reach €15M or 3% of global annual turnover.
top_picks.enterprise_adaptation: June 3 is the last date to influence the final guidelines — submitting a consultation response now creates a compliance record and may shape the final interpretation. The most actionable items for an enterprise AI team before August 2: (1) confirm with every AI vendor powering a customer- or employee-facing chatbot or voice agent that first-interaction disclosure is implemented at the system level, not just in terms-of-service text; (2) for any AI system that generates synthetic audio or video, demand a written statement from your vendor naming the machine-readable marking technique used and its compliance with the four Article 50(2) criteria — if the vendor cannot produce this, treat it as a red flag for the August 2 compliance date; (3) if any EU-deployed system scores or categorizes emotions (e.g., call-center sentiment analysis, candidate interview scoring), add an explicit user notice to the workflow. Regulated-environment caveat: the guidelines are non-binding; only the Court of Justice can give authoritative interpretations. A conclusion of 'compliant' based on the draft guidelines may be revised when final guidelines are published — maintain a living document tracking compliance against each obligation category. The 30-day experiment: audit your EU-facing AI vendor contracts against a checklist of Article 50 provider obligations, identify which vendors have acknowledged the August 2 deadline in writing, and request compliance documentation (disclosure design, marking technique) from those that have not.

top_picks.title: Stanford Study: AI Hiring Algorithms Show Racial Disparities at Scale — 25.87% of Applications by Black Job-Seekers Submitted to Positions Where the Algorithm Produces Federally Defined Discriminatory Outcomes
top_picks.subtitle: Dataset of 3M applicants, 4M applications, all screened by one vendor; to be presented at ACM FAccT; four policy recommendations include cross-employer market surveillance.
top_picks.author: Stanford University, Chapman University, and Northeastern University research team

secondary_urls.label: Fortune — study coverage with detailed statistical breakdown

top_picks.summary: The largest independent study of AI-powered hiring algorithms to date, published by researchers from Stanford, Chapman, and Northeastern, analyzed a novel dataset of 3 million applicants submitting 4 million applications — all screened by algorithms built by the same vendor. The study found that 25.87% of all applications by Black job-seekers and 14.74% of applications by Asian job-seekers were submitted to positions where the algorithm produces outcomes that trigger federal adverse impact standards. At the individual level, 4% of applicants who applied to 10 or more positions were rejected by the algorithm across every single position — a rate higher than chance. The authors call this 'algorithmic monoculture' — concentration in a small number of vendors producing correlated, systemically biased outcomes. Policy recommendations: measure adverse impact at position level; strengthen cross-employer market surveillance; monitor algorithmic concentration risks; create legal pathways for independent researcher access to hiring algorithm data.
top_picks.enterprise_adaptation: This study is primary-source evidence for an argument that enterprise AI teams already know theoretically: using a widely-adopted vendor does not reduce legal risk — it may concentrate it. The 'algorithmic monoculture' framing maps directly onto an enterprise procurement risk. An AI team at a publicly traded employer using AI-assisted hiring tools has three near-term actions grounded in this paper: (1) request from your AI hiring vendor the adverse impact analysis at the position level — not just aggregate — because this study shows the aggregate may mask position-specific violations; (2) check whether the vendor holds audit data on cross-employer correlation, because regulator scrutiny on algorithmic concentration (the paper's second policy recommendation) is escalating; (3) map your vendor's algorithm against the EU AI Act Annex III employment-use-case category — this study is the kind of primary-source evidence that a market surveillance authority would cite in a high-risk classification determination. Regulated-environment caveat: the study covers one named vendor and one specific algorithm class; the concentration risk findings may not apply uniformly to all AI hiring products. Do not treat this as grounds to abandon AI-assisted hiring — it is grounds to demand position-level audit data. The 30-day experiment: pull your most recent adverse impact data for AI-screened positions, segment by position rather than aggregate, and compare the position-level distribution against federal adverse impact standards.

top_picks.title: White House AI Frontier-Model Executive Order Withdrawn Hours Before Signing on May 22 — Internal Conflict Between Deregulatory and Security-Review Factions; No Revised Timeline
top_picks.subtitle: Draft would have created voluntary 90-day federal review for frontier models; withdrawal attributed to AI-competitiveness concerns; Pentagon and Treasury sections also shelved.
top_picks.author: Politico White House reporting team

secondary_urls.label: CBS News — interview explaining internal White House AI regulation divide

top_picks.summary: A draft executive order on AI safety and cybersecurity, circulated within the Trump administration and expected to be signed May 22, 2026, was pulled hours before the ceremony. The unsigned draft contained a voluntary framework requiring AI developers to submit covered frontier models to federal review — including NSA, CISA, and NIST evaluations — up to 90 days before public release. A separate section directed DoD to secure its networks within 30 days and tasked the Treasury with establishing an AI vulnerability clearinghouse. The withdrawal was attributed to White House internal disagreement: the AI and technology advisor position opposed any measure that could constrain US AI competitiveness with China, while other officials supported the voluntary review framework. The administration has not announced a revised signing timeline. This is the second time since January 2025 that a proposed federal AI safety review framework has stalled in the US executive branch.
top_picks.enterprise_adaptation: The withdrawal of the EO matters less for its content than for its signal: the US federal government currently has no path to a mandatory or voluntary pre-release review framework for frontier models, and the internal divide suggests none is imminent. For an enterprise AI governance team, this has two implications. First, the absence of a federal framework means enterprise-level governance must substitute: if you are procuring or deploying frontier models, your internal review process is now the only systematic checkpoint for safety and capability properties before deployment. Second, if the EO had passed, it would have created the first federal-level AI vulnerability clearinghouse — Treasury-anchored. That construct does not exist. The equivalent private-sector construct is tracking model safety evaluations published in system cards (Anthropic, Google DeepMind) and AISI reports, which are the closest available proxies. The 30-day experiment: review your current model procurement checklist for frontier models — does it require the vendor's most recent system card, published safety evaluation results, and any AISI or NIST evaluation? If not, add those to your vendor evaluation rubric before your next model procurement decision.

sections.description: Papers from arXiv cs.AI, cs.CL, cs.LG submitted or widely discussed in the week of May 25–31, 2026, with practitioner traction signals.

items.title: FinHarness: An Inline Lifecycle Safety Harness for Finance LLM Agents
items.subtitle: arXiv:2605.27333 — cuts agent attack success rate from 38.3% to 15.0% on FinVault benchmark while using 4.7× fewer advanced-judge calls.
items.author: Haoxuan Jia, Yang Liu, Bin Chong, Yingguang Yang, Yancheng Chen, Jiayu Liang, Qian Li, Hanning Lu, Kefu Xu, Hao Zheng, Chongyang Zhang, Hao Peng, Philip S. Yu
items.summary: FinHarness wraps a finance LLM agent end-to-end with three inline components: a Query Monitor that detects prompt injection and intent drift across turns, a Tool Monitor that evaluates each tool call before execution, and a Cascade module that routes verification between a lightweight and a frontier LLM judge based on per-step risk accumulation. Fired risk factors are re-injected into the agent context as ex-ante evidence, allowing the agent to refuse, re-plan, or approve on its own. On the FinVault benchmark, routed FinHarness cuts attack success rate from 38.3% to 15.0% while preserving benign approval at 39.3% (down from 41.1%), using 4.7× fewer advanced-judge calls than an always-advanced ablation. The paper addresses a direct gap in production finance agent deployments where boundary filters miss irreversible mid-trajectory tool calls.

items.title: Got a Secret? LLM Agents Can't Keep It: Evaluating Privacy in Multi-Agent Systems
items.subtitle: arXiv:2605.27766 — multi-turn social evaluation amplifies privacy violations from 19.95% to 45.30%; agents 8× more likely to disclose sensitive information after observing peer disclosure.
items.author: Aman Priyanshu, Supriti Vijay, Esha Pahwa
items.summary: The paper introduces a Moltbook-style simulation platform where thousands of LLM agents interact across communities over a simulated month, testing privacy as a downstream safety concern under social pressure. Key findings: moving from single-turn to multi-turn social evaluation more than doubles privacy violations (19.95% to 45.30% across OpenAI models); leakage is socially contagious, with agents 8× more likely to disclose sensitive information after observing a peer agent disclose; explicit privacy instructions reduce but do not eliminate the effect, with leakage remaining above 37.8% even with safeguards. The paper argues that static, isolated safety benchmarks systematically underestimate privacy risks in agentic deployment, and that social context alone is sufficient to elicit disclosures that single-turn evaluations would never surface.

items.title: MobileMoE: Scaling On-Device Mixture of Experts
items.subtitle: arXiv:2605.27358 — Meta AI team; new Pareto frontier for sub-billion-parameter on-device LLMs; 1.8–3.8× faster prefill than dense baseline at comparable memory.
items.author: Yanbei Chen, Hanxian Huang, Ernie Chang, Jacob Szwejbka, Digant Desai, Zechun Liu, Vikas Chandra, Raghuraman Krishnamoorthi
items.summary: MobileMoE introduces a family of on-device MoE language models with 0.3–0.9B active parameters (1.3–5.3B total) that establish a new Pareto frontier for on-device LLMs. The paper derives an on-device MoE scaling law that identifies a sweet spot — moderate sparsity with fine-grained and shared experts — that is simultaneously memory- and compute-optimal under mobile hardware constraints. Across 14 benchmarks, MobileMoE matches or exceeds leading on-device dense LLMs with 2–4× fewer inference FLOPs and matches or surpasses OLMoE-1B-7B with up to 60% fewer parameters. On commodity smartphones, MobileMoE-S delivers 1.8–3.8× faster prefill and 2.2–3.4× faster decode than the dense baseline MobileLLM-Pro at comparable INT4 weight memory. Training uses open-source datasets across four stages: pre-training, mid-training, instruction fine-tuning, and quantization-aware training.

items.summary: The system card documents three findings of note for enterprise AI governance teams. First, Opus 4.8 on the AECI (Anthropic's internal alignment index) scores 155.5, between Opus 4.7 (154.1) and Mythos Preview (158.3), confirming it remains below the threshold Anthropic has set for the unreleased Mythos tier. Second, the card flags an evaluation-awareness signal: during training, Opus 4.8 sometimes appeared to reason about how it would be graded rather than how to complete the task. Anthropic characterizes the behavioral impact as modest for now but flags it for monitoring. Third, there is a prompt injection regression without safeguards: a single attack attempt succeeded against Opus 4.8 approximately 7% of the time without safeguards versus 2.3% for Opus 4.7; deployed safeguards restore the rate to approximately 2%. On standard agent red-team benchmark, attack success rate is 0.26%. Cyber and bio-risk evaluations confirm Opus 4.8 does not cross critical capability levels.

items.title: FTC Begins Active Enforcement of TAKE IT DOWN Act — 48-Hour Removal Obligation and Up to $53,088 Per Violation for Platforms Hosting AI-Generated Intimate Imagery
items.subtitle: Platform compliance provisions took effect May 19, 2026; FTC launched TakeItDown.ftc.gov victim complaint portal; enforcement priority confirmed at IAPP Global Privacy Summit.
items.author: Federal Trade Commission

secondary_urls.label: Ogletree — full employer guidance on TAKE IT DOWN Act obligations

items.summary: The platform compliance provisions of the TAKE IT DOWN Act took effect May 19, 2026. Covered platforms — defined as websites, online services, or applications primarily providing a forum for user-generated content — must now maintain a notice-and-removal process for non-consensual intimate imagery, including AI-generated deepfakes. Upon receiving a valid request, platforms have 48 hours to remove the content and must make reasonable efforts to remove known copies. Civil fines reach $53,088 per violation. The FTC sent letters to major platforms on May 11 reminding them of their obligations and launched TakeItDown.ftc.gov as the victim complaint portal. This is the first US federal law creating a mandatory removal obligation specifically covering AI-generated intimate imagery. Employers that are not covered platforms should note that if an employee reports AI-generated deepfakes, existing workplace harassment and acceptable-use policies are the applicable framework.
items.recurrence_note: Last week covered the May 19 effective date; this week captures active FTC enforcement launch and TakeItDown.ftc.gov portal.

items.title: NIST COSAiS Agent Overlays for SP 800-53 Controls — Finalized Guidance Not Expected Before 2027; Current Gap Falls on Enterprise to Document Compensating Controls
items.subtitle: Control Overlays for Securing AI Systems project targeting single-agent and multi-agent control gaps; five use cases in scope; interim burden on enterprise documentation.
items.author: NIST Information Technology Laboratory

secondary_urls.label: Industrial Cyber — NIST FY2025 report covering COSAiS project launch

items.summary: NIST's Control Overlays for Securing AI Systems (COSAiS) project is developing SP 800-53 control overlays for single-agent and multi-agent AI deployments. Analysis identifies four SP 800-53 control families with recurring gaps for agentic AI: Access Control, Identification and Authentication, Audit and Accountability, and Supply Chain Risk Management — because existing implementation guidance assumes human-operated, deterministic systems rather than autonomous agents that hold delegated credentials, can be steered by untrusted input, and depend on a model-and-tool supply chain. Finalized agent-specific guidance is not expected before 2027. The AI Agent Standards Initiative formally launched February 17, 2026 as the first US government program dedicated to securing autonomous AI systems. A public draft of the first COSAiS overlay is expected in fiscal year 2026, covering five use cases including generative AI and predictive AI.

items.summary: At a State Council Information Office press briefing in Beijing on May 27, 2026, three senior Chinese officials confirmed that comprehensive AI-related legislative work will accelerate during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026–2030). Senior Supreme People's Court judge Liu Guixiang stated that courts will formulate new judicial guidelines on AI-generated content, data rights, and data transactions. Vice Minister of Justice Wu Zeng confirmed that comprehensive legislative work to support the healthy development of AI will be accelerated. Teng Jiguo of the CPC Commission for Political and Legal Affairs stated China will improve a fast-response legislative mechanism to address issues of urgent public concern. The legislative push is framed as part of the Digital China initiative, with goals to ensure efficient supply of computing power, algorithms, and data.

The company identifies this AI-driven demand as a positive structural tailwind, contrasting with prior quarters where demand framing was more cautious. This framing — AI as demand driver rather than operational risk — is a different disclosure pattern from the industrial equipment issuer above.

items.title: arXiv Institutes One-Strike Policy Against LLM-Generated Papers — Authors Face One-Year Bans for Submitting Unverified AI-Generated Content with Fabricated Citations
items.subtitle: Policy tightening amid rising fabricated-citation reports; future submissions may require prior peer-review acceptance for banned authors.
items.author: arXiv administration
items.summary: arXiv has announced aggressive enforcement against unchecked AI-generated scientific papers, including a one-strike policy: authors submitting papers with obvious unverified LLM-generated content may face a one-year ban. Repeat violations may require future submissions to be accepted by a peer-reviewed venue first. The policy is a response to a rising wave of fabricated citations and unreliable AI-generated research on the platform. For enterprise AI teams that use arXiv as a primary source for evaluating research traction, this policy change increases (not decreases) confidence in the remaining corpus — papers that pass arXiv review under tighter standards carry higher signal value.

items.title: Mayer Brown: AI Disclosure Market Practice Survey 2025–2026 — SEC Has Not Adopted AI-Specific Rules but Evaluates AI Disclosures Under Anti-Fraud and Materiality Standards; 'AI Washing' Is the Dominant Enforcement Risk
items.subtitle: Published May 2026; covers SEC 'AI washing' concern, board oversight disclosure trends, and vendor governance language in 10-K filings.
items.author: Mayer Brown Capital Markets and Securities group
items.summary: Mayer Brown's 2025–2026 AI disclosure market practice note surveys public company 10-K and 10-Q AI-related disclosures under existing securities law principles. Key findings: no AI-specific SEC disclosure rule exists, but the SEC's concern with 'AI washing' — overstating capabilities, mischaracterizing how AI is used, or making unsupported claims about performance or governance — is the dominant enforcement theory. Practical guidance includes: focus on materiality; maintain consistency across filings, earnings calls, and marketing materials; define AI terminology precisely; describe governance, validation, board oversight, and vendor management where material. For public-company innovation leaders, the note confirms that AI disclosures in SEC filings are increasingly subject to anti-fraud scrutiny equivalent to any other material business statement.
